nodes.name: NF Pretreatment
nodes.procedure: Commercial NF (2 cm×3 cm) was cleaned by sequentially sonicating in 3 M HCl solution for 15 min to remove surface oxides and impurities and then rinsed with deionized water and ethanol for 15 min to wash the residual acid.
nodes.source_text: Pretreatment of Nickel Foam (NF). First, commercial NF (2 cm×3 cm) was cleaned by sequentially sonicating in 3 M HCl solution for 15 min...

nodes.name: Hydrothermal Ru-Ni(OH)₂ Synthesis
nodes.procedure: 20 mg of RuCl₃ was dissolved in 30 mL of ethanol. After vigorous stirring at room temperature for 30 min, the obtained solution was transferred to a 50 mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave with the pretreated NF and reacted at 120°C for 10 h. After the reaction was over, Ru-Ni(OH)₂/NF was obtained, washed with ethanol, and further vacuum-dried at 60°C overnight. The calculated mass loading of Ru-Ni(OH)₂ was about 0.8 mg cm⁻². The microscopic redox reaction is 2RuCl₃ + 3Ni + 6C₂H₅OH → 2Ru + 3Ni(OH)₂ + 6C₂H₅OH↑.

nodes.name: Electrochemical Activation
nodes.procedure: The Ru-Ni(OH)2/NF precursor, Hg/HgO, and a graphite rod were used as the working, reference, and counter electrodes, respectively. Then, 100 cyclic voltammetry (CV) cycles from 0.6 to 0.8 V vs Hg/HgO in 1 M KOH solution were carried out at a scan rate of 50 mV s⁻¹. The resulting electrode, named R-Ru-Ni(OH)2/NF, was directly used as the working electrode for subsequent electrochemical measurements.

nodes.name: Pt/C Electrode Preparation
nodes.procedure: 5 mg of commercial 20% Pt/C was uniformly dispersed in a mixture solution containing 440 μL of ethanol, 40 μL of water, and 20 μL of Nafion solution. After continuous sonication for 1 h, the homogeneous catalyst ink was dropped onto nickel foam (working area: 0.5 cm×0.5 cm) with a controlled load of about 0.81 mg cm⁻², which directly served as the working electrode after drying in air overnight.

nodes.characterization_summary: Both Ru-Ni(OH)₂ and R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ show hexagonal Ru crystalline substance (PDF#06-0663) with no significant changes after activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: XRD patterns show that before and after activation, the catalyst forms a hexagonal Ru crystalline substance (PDF#06-0663) (Figure S2).

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM reveals uniform nanoparticles with rough surface and no obvious pinholes; no significant morphological changes after activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: SEM and TEM images reveal the core-shell nanostructure of Ru-Ni(OH)₂. It is apparent that the nanoparticles with a rough surface are uniform in size, and no obvious pinholes can be observed (Figure 1b, Figure S3).

properties.description: Gray scale TEM image of nanoparticles

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru core diameter 80-100 nm, Ni(OH)₂ shell thickness 20 nm before activation; shell thickness slightly decreases after CV activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ru core diameter and Ni(OH)₂ shell thickness are approximately 80-100 and 20 nm, respectively. No significant morphological changes can be found after electrochemical activation (Figure 1c, Figure S4).

nodes.characterization_summary: Lattice fringes of 0.214 nm (Ru (002)) and 0.233 nm (Ni(OH)₂ (101)) before activation; mainly Ru crystal structure after activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: HRTEM images indicate that the thickness of the Ni(OH)₂ shell slightly decreases after CV activation... well-defined lattice fringe spacings of 0.214 and 0.233 nm near the shell of Ru-Ni(OH)₂ correspond to the (002) crystal plane of Ru and the (101) plane of Ni(OH)₂.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru elements primarily inside nanospheres, Ni and O mainly on surface, confirming Ru core-Ni(OH)₂ shell structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping results exhibit that Ru elements are primarily located inside the Ru-Ni(OH)₂ nanospheres, while Ni and O are mainly distributed on the surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru content 0.70 wt% (0.352 mg cm⁻² NF), no significant change before/after activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: ICP-OES, XPS, and EDS analyses of Ru content reveal that the Ru content in Ru-Ni(OH)₂ is relatively low (0.70 wt %, 0.352 mg cm⁻² NF) and does not change significantly before and after activation (Table S1).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni 2p binding energies shift negatively by 0.6 eV, Ru 3p positively by 0.45 eV after activation; increased O 1s peak areas at ~531.3 and 532.7 eV indicate more surface OH groups.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The comparison reveals that the binding energies of Ni 2p₃/₂ and Ni 2p₁/₂ orbitals negatively shift by about 0.6 eV after activation, while the binding energies of Ru 3p₃/₂ and Ru 3p₁/₂ orbitals positively shift by about 0.45 eV... increase of the O 1s peak areas located at ∼531.3 and 532.7 eV also proves the presence of more surface OH groups.

nodes.characterization_summary: Mass loss at ~300°C for R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ attributed to evaporation of surface water and hydroxyl species.
nodes.evidence_snippet: TG curves (Figure 2d) show a mass loss process at around 300°C for the activated R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂/NF, which is attributed to the evaporation of surface water and hydroxyl species.

nodes.characterization_summary: R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ shows stronger hydroxyl radical EPR signal indicating formation of chemical hydroxyl groups (OH_ad) after activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: EPR spectra prove that the R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ catalyst has a stronger hydroxyl radical EPR signal (Figure 2e), indicating the formation of chemical hydroxyl groups (OH_ad) after electrochemical activation.

nodes.characterization_summary: H₂ desorption peak temperature lower for R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ (400.69°C) vs Ru-Ni(OH)₂ (502.26°C), indicating better H₂ desorption.
nodes.evidence_snippet: H₂-TPD shows that the H₂ desorption peak temperature of R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ is lower (400.69°C) than that of Ru-Ni(OH)₂ (502.26°C).

nodes.characterization_summary: Valence band maximum of R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ is 4.44 eV vs 3.37 eV for Ru-Ni(OH)₂.
nodes.evidence_snippet: UPS reveals that the valence band maximum of R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ was calculated to be 4.44 eV higher than the 3.37 eV of Ru-Ni(OH)₂.

nodes.characterization_summary: Electrochemical double-layer capacitance C_dl = 27.3 mF cm⁻² for R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ (higher than Ru-Ni(OH)₂), used for ECSA calculation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ has... larger C_dl value (27.3 mF cm⁻²) compared to Ru-Ni(OH)₂, indicating... increase of the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA).

nodes.characterization_summary: R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ shows pronounced *OH bending vibration peak at 749 cm⁻¹ that intensifies with voltage.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In situ Raman spectroscopy confirms that... R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ exhibits a more pronounced *OH bending vibration peak at 749 cm⁻¹ after activation, which intensifies with the application of voltage.

nodes.characterization_summary: Peaks at 871 cm⁻¹ (O-H bending of *OH) and 1013 cm⁻¹ (Ru-OH stretching of OH_ad); ¹⁸O-labeling shows red shift confirming Ru-OH_ad sites.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Significant absorption peaks... at 871 and 1013 cm⁻¹ in the spectra of R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂, corresponding to the O–H bending vibration of the *OH intermediate and the Ru–OH stretching vibration of OH_ad.

nodes.characterization_summary: R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ shows smaller charge transfer resistance R_ct = 4.7 ± 0.5 Ω compared to Ru-Ni(OH)₂.
nodes.evidence_snippet: R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ has... smaller charge transfer resistance (R_ct) (4.7±0.5Ω)... indicating... promotion of catalytic kinetics and charge transfer capability.

nodes.characterization_summary: R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ water contact angle ~0° with permeation time 0.473 s (vs 0.542 s for Ru-Ni(OH)₂), indicating superior hydrophilicity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Water droplets quickly spread, absorb, and break on the surface of R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂, with a water CA of ∼0°. Typically, the time required... is shorter (0.473 vs 0.542 s).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ex situ Raman shows enhanced Ru-OH vibration peaks in R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ verifying more bound water and hydroxyl species.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Enhancement of the Ru-OH vibration peaks in ex situ Raman and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy further verifies the existence of more bound water and hydroxyl species in the R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ex situ FTIR shows enhanced Ru-OH vibration peaks in R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂ verifying more bound water and hydroxyl species.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Enhancement of the Ru-OH vibration peaks in ex situ Raman and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy further verifies the existence of more bound water and hydroxyl species in the R-Ru-Ni(OH)₂.
